newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-SLANEY INVESTIGATED OVER DRUG TEST.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-SLANEY INVESTIGATED OVER DRUG TEST.

text.p: Women's distance star Mary Slaney has been investigated by the IAAF and has a U.S. hearing pending over a drug test at last year's U.S. Olympic trials, her attorney said Thursday, expressing "outrage" at the handling of the case.
The 38-year-old Slaney has not been suspended and "there has not been a positive drug test," attorney Doriane Lambelet Coleman said in a telephone interview from her Durham, North Carolina, office.
"Mary has never taken testosterone or any steroids."
Coleman, a Duke University law professor, said she and Slaney were outraged at the lack of a resolution of the case almost one year after the drug test.
The investigation and pending hearing centres around a higher than acceptable ratio of testosterone, a naturally occurring male harmone, discovered in a drug test of Slaney last June, Coleman said.
U.S. athletics officials declined to comment, citing the confidentiality of the case.
An athlete may be suspended under IAAF and IOC rules when the ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone is found to be above 6-to-1.
Slaney's level in the Atlanta test was higher than 6-to-1, Coleman said, "But there has not been a suspension and we do not expect her to be suspended.
"She is competing now and we fully expect her to compete in the U.S. and world championships. Mary has been tested a zillion times before this and after this and she has never tested positive."

Slaney, making a comeback after numerous injuries, finished seventh in her preliminary race of the women's 5,000 meters at the Atlanta Olympics and was a close second in a spirited women's 1,500 meters at the world indoor championships in Paris in March.

"We did not want this to drag on into the outdoor season," Coleman said, noting that a telephonic hearing by U.S. officials in February had been delayed because legal representatives of the U.S. federation were not prepared to continue.
"It is very difficult for Mary to compete under this cloud," she added.

Coleman said she was convinced Slaney would not receive a fair hearing before a U.S. hearing panel currently assigned to the case because, she said, it had leaked details of the investigation and hearing to the U.S. media.
"They have taken the law into their own hands," she said.
